story.title: La comanda de la mesa seis
story.teaser: Friday night at a Buenos Aires steakhouse: the boss hates mistakes, and one small order ticket is about to cause a big one.
lines: Es viernes en Buenos Aires.
It's Friday in Buenos Aires.
Delfina es cocinera en una parrilla.
Delfina is a cook at a parrilla, a steakhouse.
A las nueve, tiene tres mesas: cinco bifes, dos ensaladas.
At nine, she has three tables: five steaks, two salads.
Su jefe, don Horacio, es serio: no le gustan los errores.
Her boss, Don Horacio, is stern: he doesn't like mistakes.
— ¡Faltan diez minutos! —dice el mozo.
"Ten minutes to go!" says the waiter.
Otra comanda: mesa seis, «9 bifes».
Another order ticket: table six, "9 steaks".
Delfina pone nueve en la parrilla.
Delfina puts nine on the grill.
Don Horacio mira a Delfina: —¡La mesa seis tiene seis personas!
Don Horacio looks at Delfina: "Table six has six people!"
¡La comanda está al revés!
The ticket is upside down!
El mozo ve a tres clientes nuevos.
The waiter sees three new customers.
— ¿Tienen bifes? ¡Nos gustan mucho!
"Do you have steaks? We love them!"
— ¡Tres, listos!
"Three, ready to go!"
A las doce: ¡son cien bifes!
At twelve: that's a hundred steaks!
Don Horacio prueba uno y mira a Delfina.
Don Horacio tastes one and looks at Delfina.
— Me gusta tu bife. Y sonríe.
"I like your steak." And he smiles.
vocab: to be left, to go (faltan diez minutos = ten minutes to go)
upside down; the wrong way round
to like (me gusta / no le gustan / nos gustan)

quiz.q: ¿Cuántas personas hay en la mesa seis?
¿Por qué Delfina pone nueve bifes en la parrilla?
options: Hay nueve personas en la mesa seis

quiz.q: ¿Para quién son los tres bifes de más?
En «¡La comanda está al revés!», ¿qué significa «al revés»?

story.prompt: What food do you like, and what don't you like? Write 2-3 sentences in Spanish in the present tense. Use gusta for one thing and gustan for more than one, and add one sentence with tener (for example: Me gustan los bifes. No me gusta la ensalada. Tengo un restaurante favorito.).

concepts.grammar: ser for days, jobs, descriptions and totals (Es viernes; es cocinera; es serio; son cien bifes); gustar (no le gustan los errores; nos gustan; me gusta tu bife); tener (tiene tres mesas; tiene seis personas; ¿Tienen bifes?); personal a (mira a Delfina; ve a tres clientes).
concepts.vocabulary: Restaurant kitchen words from Argentina (parrilla, bife, mozo, comanda, cliente) and numbers 1–12 plus cien.
concepts.skills: Following numbers and counts in a short story; spotting a visual clue (a 6 read upside down).

grammar.explain: Use 'ser' for the day (Es viernes), for jobs (Delfina es cocinera), for what someone is like (Don Horacio es serio), and for prices and totals (¿Cuánto es? Son cien). The verb agrees with the amount: es un bife, son cien bifes. Watch out: for jobs, Spanish drops 'un/una': es cocinera, not 'es una cocinera'.
examples: Es viernes en Buenos Aires.
It's Friday in Buenos Aires.
Delfina es cocinera en una parrilla.
Delfina is a cook at a steakhouse.
Su jefe, don Horacio, es serio.
Her boss, Don Horacio, is stern.
A las doce: ¡son cien bifes!
At twelve: that's a hundred steaks!

grammar.explain: 'Gustar' works like 'to please': the thing you like is the subject. Use 'gusta' for one thing and 'gustan' for plural things. The person goes before: me (to me), te (to you), le (to him/her), nos (to us). Watch out: don't say 'yo gusto' or 'le gusta los errores'.
examples: Don Horacio es serio: no le gustan los errores.
Don Horacio is stern: he doesn't like mistakes.
— ¿Tienen bifes? ¡Nos gustan mucho!
"Do you have steaks? We love them!"
— Me gusta tu bife.
"I like your steak."

grammar.explain: 'Tener' (to have) is irregular: tengo, tienes, tiene, tenemos, tienen. Use it for what someone has: tres mesas, seis personas. To say you don't have something, put 'no' before the verb: no tengo dinero. Watch out: 'tenemos' (we have) has no 'ie', and Spanish usually drops un/una after 'no': no tengo mesa.
examples: A las nueve, tiene tres mesas.
At nine, she has three tables.
¡La mesa seis tiene seis personas!
Table six has six people!
— ¿Tienen bifes? —Sí, tenemos tres.
"Do you have steaks?" "Yes, we have three."

grammar.explain: When a specific person receives the action (is seen, looked at, called), Spanish puts 'a' before them. This 'a' is not translated. Things don't take it: mira a Delfina, but mira la comanda. Watch out: a + el becomes al: Delfina mira al jefe.
examples: Don Horacio mira a Delfina.
Don Horacio looks at Delfina.
El mozo ve a tres clientes nuevos.
The waiter sees three new customers.
Delfina mira la comanda.
Delfina looks at the order ticket. (no 'a': a ticket is a thing)

gq.q: Fill in the blank: A las doce, ¡___ cien bifes!
gq.why: Totals and prices use ser, and the verb agrees with the amount: cien bifes is plural, so 'son'. English says 'that's a hundred', but Spanish does not say 'es cien bifes'.

gq.q: Don Horacio doesn't like mistakes (plural). Which sentence is correct?
gq.why: With gustar, the thing liked is the subject. 'Los errores' is plural, so the verb is 'gustan'; 'le' (to him) goes before the verb.

gq.q: Complete: La mesa seis ___ seis personas.
gq.why: La mesa (it) takes the él/ella form: tiene. 'Hay' can't follow a subject like 'la mesa seis'; you could say 'En la mesa seis hay seis personas'.

gq.q: Which sentence needs the personal 'a' in the blank?
options: Delfina pone ___ nueve bifes en la parrilla.
gq.why: Personal 'a' goes before a specific person who receives the action: mira a Delfina. La comanda and los bifes are things, so they take no 'a'.

gq.q: How do you say 'Delfina is a cook'?
gq.why: Jobs use ser, and Spanish usually drops 'un/una' before a job: Delfina es cocinera.

gq.q: Complete: Me ___ tu bife, pero no me ___ las ensaladas.
gq.why: The verb agrees with the thing liked: tu bife (one) → gusta; las ensaladas (plural) → gustan. 'Gusto' would mean 'I please'.

gq.q: How does Delfina say 'We have three steaks ready'?
gq.why: Tener changes e→ie only in some forms (tengo is irregular, tienes, tiene, tienen). The 'we' form keeps the e: tenemos. 'Tengo' means 'I have'.

gq.q: How do you say 'The waiter sees the boss'?
options: El mozo ve a el jefe.
gq.why: The boss is a specific person, so he takes personal 'a', and a + el always joins to 'al': ve al jefe.

steps.say: ¡Hola! Soy Delfina. Soy cocinera en una parrilla de Buenos Aires.
steps.en: Hi! I'm Delfina. I'm a cook at a steakhouse in Buenos Aires.
r: Hi, Delfina! Do you like your job?

steps.say: Es un restaurante de carne. Hoy es viernes y tengo muchas mesas. ¿Te gustan los bifes?
steps.en: It's a meat restaurant. Today is Friday and I have a lot of tables. Do you like steaks?
r: Yes, I like them a lot.

steps.say: Mi jefe, don Horacio, es muy serio. No le gustan los errores. Y a las nueve tengo un problema.
steps.en: My boss, Don Horacio, is very stern. He doesn't like mistakes. And at nine I have a problem.

steps.say: La comanda de la mesa seis dice nueve bifes. Pongo nueve en la parrilla. Pero la comanda está al revés.
steps.en: The ticket for table six says nine steaks. I put nine on the grill. But the ticket is upside down.
r: It's a six, not a nine!
How many people does table six have?

steps.say: Sí, seis personas y nueve bifes. Pero el mozo ve a tres clientes nuevos. ¿Qué hago?
steps.en: Yes, six people and nine steaks. But the waiter sees three new customers. What do I do?
r: Los tres bifes son para ellos.
The three steaks are for them.

steps.say: ¡Sí! Y don Horacio prueba un bife y dice: me gusta tu bife. ¡Y sonríe!
steps.en: Yes! And Don Horacio tastes a steak and says: I like your steak. And he smiles!

culture.landmark: Puente de la Mujer, Puerto Madero
culture.caption: Puerto Madero's old brick docks are lined with restaurants, many of them parrillas, and crossed by the white Puente de la Mujer footbridge.
culture.prompt: Argentine setting. Location: Buenos Aires, Argentina. The famous landmark Puente de la Mujer, Puerto Madero must be clearly visible and recognizable in the image. A busy Friday night inside a classic porteño parrilla: a big open charcoal grill with glowing embers and steaks sizzling on the iron bars, a steel counter with plates of bife de chorizo, green salads and small bowls of chimichurri, paper order tickets clipped to a rail above the counter, a round kitchen clock on a white-tiled wall. Through the large front window, the red-brick warehouses of Puerto Madero along the dock and the white mast of the Puente de la Mujer lit up at night. No people.
